transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-01-10 16:00 PST
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Recording: Fireflies auto
- Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Samir (Redwood Solutions), Jared (HorizonTech CTO), Priya (ML Lead), Evan (Infra), Lea (Security)

Auto-summary (auto sections may be noisy):
- Quick ask: what deployment for 200-1,000 concurrent real-time summarization users; p95 and streaming token latency matters; want predictable tails for regulatory SLA.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros?
[00:06] Jared (HorizonTech): Jared here, CTO. Priya leading the ML side, Evan infrastructure, Lea on security.
[00:12] Priya (HorizonTech): Hi, good to meet you. We're evaluating Redwood for our summarization endpoint, mostly real-time streams from our web clients.
[00:18] Alex (Redwood): Great. High-level can you share current numbers — p95, concurrent users, tokens per request?
[00:26] Priya: Sure. Our typical summarized doc is 600 tokens, average response ~350 tokens. Peak concurrent active writers is about 300, but we want headroom for 1k concurrent. Production p95 target we like is 200-220ms for token streaming to UI, end-to-end.
[00:40] Maya (Redwood): When you say '200ms p95', you're referring to token emission latency for streaming, or end-to-end response completion?
[00:48] Priya: Token emission for the UI. We show incremental tokens as they arrive. End-to-end isn't as strict, but we'd still like overall generation not to exceed 3s in normal cases.
[00:57] Evan: Also want predictable tails when we have bursts — we run a lot during daytime events, spikes can go 2-3x baseline in <30s.
[01:06] Samir (Redwood): Got it. Two axes here: per-token latency (streaming path) and throughput (tokens/sec per instance and aggregate). We should profile both short sequence streaming and longer runs.
[01:18] Jared: Right, and we care about deployment options. Hosted is easier but we need guarantees. Dedicated reserved pools look appealing. Also private VPC option for data residency.
[01:29] Lea (Security): For us SOC 2 and KMS integration are must-haves. Also audit logs for token retention and access.
[01:36] Maya: That aligns with Redwood Private / Dedicated offerings. For P95 tails we often recommend dedicated since noisy neighbors in hosted can bump tails, but we can show benchmark data.
[01:46] Priya: How much throughput can one dedicated GPU give us for our model? We're using a Llama-2 derivative (~13B) quantized to 4-bit in-house variant.
[01:56] Maya: Depends on sequence length and quant kernel. Ballpark: for 13B quantized on A100-like instance you might see steady-state 250-600 tokens/sec depending on batch size and KV cache reuse. For streaming with low-latency single-user, per-token latency is more sensitive — p95 might be 120-250ms single-threaded.
[02:12] Priya: Our users are interactive, so low latency single-stream is critical. Concurrency target 1k means we need many concurrent low-latency streams. How do you handle concurrency?
[02:22] Maya: Continuous batching and smart routing. We can route by latency SLO or cost. For 1k concurrent short streams we'll likely need autoscaling with many small workers pinned for low-latency. Dedicated pools avoid noisy neighbor but you still need planning for prefix cache expiration and KV cache warmups.
[02:35] Evan: Curious about token/sec sustained. If each request emits 350 tokens at ~20 requests/sec across the fleet, that is... math.
[02:44] Jared: Our rough estimate: 1k concurrent users * average 0.5 req/min? Hmm. Let's not get lost in calc here. We will provide a traffic profile.
[02:53] Priya: We'll provide seq length distribution and concurrency curve.
[02:56] Maya: Good. For benchmarks we'll want representative prompt prefixes and KV cache reuse rates — cache hits change per-token work substantially.
[03:05] Jared: What's your definition of p95 here? Is that from request arrival to first token or token emission?
[03:13] Alex: We can measure both. Redwood's telemetry can break down token-level latency, model compute, kernel selection, network hop times. We'll share a profiling template.
[03:23] Lea: On security, we will need KMS details, HSM conversation, and log retention. Can you confirm private deployment options support customer-managed KMS?
[03:33] Samir: Yes, private deployment supports customer KMS and HSM integrations. Dedicated hosted mode supports encryption at rest and customer-managed keys in certain tiers. We'll include exact docs.
[03:43] Priya: About streaming, do you support per-token websocket streaming to minimize tail? We want as soon as token is ready push to client.
[03:50] Maya: We support streaming over websockets and chunked HTTP, and we expose server-side latency metrics. The streaming pipeline tries to flush partial tokens fast — for short sequences this is critical. There's some overhead for each flush, so we tune flush sizes.
[04:06] Evan: Benchmark question: how do you simulate bursty traffic? We run 3x traffic spikes for 30s. Will Redwood's benchmark harness do that?
[04:14] Maya: We have a harness that can replay traces and simulate bursts, including cold-starts and KV cache miss ratios. For dedicated tests we can provision a test cluster isolated for the window.
[04:24] Priya: For p95 <= 220ms, is that feasible for streams at scale? What are realistic expectations?
[04:30] Maya: For single-token emission p95 200-220ms is ambitious but achievable with dedicated pools and warmed KV caches; depends heavily on model size, quantization, and whether the request can be batched. At 1k concurrent truly low-latency streams you'll need substantial reserved capacity and autoscaling headroom.
[04:45] Jared: If we do dedicated, what headroom do we plan for? 50% above baseline?
[04:50] Samir: Typical recommendation: 1.5-2x headroom for 99th percentile under burst profiles. We can run stress tests to find empirical headroom.
[04:59] Lea: On compliance — are there options for on-prem air-gapped deployment? We may have regulated customers.
[05:05] Samir: Yes, Redwood Private supports air-gapped installations; Ops will do an onboarding runbook. We'll provide the package and requirements.
[05:13] Priya: About cost — can you ballpark hosted vs dedicated for our expected throughput?
[05:18] Alex: We'll give an initial TCO: hosted per-token plus a small premium for low-latency SLOs; dedicated has monthly reserved commit. We'll run a cost model once you give typical token volumes and concurrency profile.
[05:27] Jared: Also how do you handle fallbacks? If dedicated pool saturates, do you have fallback to hosted model variants?
[05:34] Maya: Yes, smart routing can failover to compatible model variants in another region or to hosted overflow. Policy controls let you prefer latency or cost and set hard caps.
[05:42] Evan: One technical deep-dive request: we want kernel metrics and exact sequence length distribution mapping to tokens/sec. Can Redwood share kernel-level profiles?
[05:51] Maya: We can share aggregated kernel timing and a best-effort mapping; exact GPU kernel internals are somewhat sensitive but we'll provide sufficient profile data: per-token compute, attention kernel timing, memory footprints.
[06:02] Priya: For the in-house 13B quant model, what about quantized kernels and accuracy regressions? We don't want quality drops.
[06:09] Maya: We'll recommend quantization profiles and run evals on your prompt set to ensure output parity. Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring and regression alerts.
[06:19] Jared: Ok practical next steps?
[06:22] Alex: We'll send the profiling template and pricing. Maya will draft the benchmark plan. We'll schedule a 2-hr dedicated benchmark window. You'll provide test dataset and traffic trace. Lea will get the security pack.
[06:34] Priya: Sounds good. A couple more quick clarifications: do you have per-route quotas and throttles?
[06:40] Samir: Yes, token-level rate limiting, per-route quotas and token cost breakdowns in the console.
[06:46] Lea: Also need RBAC and SSO for our team.
[06:50] Alex: Redwood supports SAML SSO and RBAC controls. We'll include docs.
[06:56] Jared: Great. If dedicated looks like the right fit we'll plan a pilot.
[07:00] Alex: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with dates and artifacts.

End of transcript.
